source_doc.title: Portfolio Projects 2027
source_doc.note: Private to the owner's claude.ai account. The doc is the source of truth; this file is a structured copy of its Overview tab.

intro: Nine projects, built in order, that add up to the profile NVIDIA's AI Computing, GPU Computing, Autonomous Driving and AI Agent roles hire for: you can make a model run fast on a GPU, scale it, serve it, wrap it in a reliable agent, and prove it with numbers.
focus_note: Projects 1, 2 and 5 matter most for the AI Computing, Kernel Libraries and AI Agent internships. If time runs short, finish those three to a high standard before starting the others.

rules.title: README with a results table first
rules.detail: Numbers against a named baseline (llama.cpp, cuBLAS, vLLM, etcd), the hardware and how to reproduce them.

rules.title: Design doc
rules.detail: docs/DESIGN.md, 2–4 pages: goal, non-goals, architecture diagram, key decisions with the alternatives rejected, known limits.

rules.title: Benchmarks as code
rules.detail: One command reruns them; results are committed as CSV so the charts in the README can be regenerated.

rules.title: Tests and CI
rules.detail: Correctness tests against a reference implementation (PyTorch, a spec, a model checker), run in GitHub Actions on every push.

rules.title: Write-up
rules.detail: One long blog post per project on your site, explaining what was hard and what the profiler showed. Recruiters and referrers read these.

rules.title: Demo video
rules.detail: A 2-minute demo video, linked from the README.

habits: Two habits make the portfolio stand out. First, always report a number against a strong baseline, even when you lose. Second, upstream something: a bug fix or small feature merged into vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, CUTLASS or Triton is worth more on a CV than another solo project.
overrun_rule: If a project runs 50% over its estimate, cut its stretch goals rather than the next project.
time_note: Estimates are full-time weeks at about 8 h a day; estHours counts a week as 7 days (56 h), and milestone hours are rough splits of it. The plan keeps about 4 of the 8 daily hours on projects and the rest on courses.

projects.title: nanoserve: an LLM inference engine from scratch
projects.table_title: nanoserve: LLM inference engine from scratch
projects.summary: A single-GPU engine that loads a real open model (Llama 3.2 1B/3B or Qwen3 1.7B/4B) and serves it through an OpenAI-compatible API, with every hot path written by you.
projects.proves: You understand every layer of LLM inference
projects.why: Inference is the largest GPU workload in 2027, and teams hire people who know where the milliseconds go. Wrappers around vLLM are common; an engine whose paged KV cache, scheduler and kernels you wrote yourself, benchmarked against llama.cpp and vLLM, is rare at intern level.

schedule.what: Milestones 1–2 (correct forward pass, KV cache and decode loop), alongside Project 2
Finish: continuous batching and fast kernels, bringing over the Project 2 kernels
Polish, write-up and demo video before applying

milestones.title: Correct forward pass
milestones.detail: Load safetensors weights, run the model in C++/CUDA with naive kernels, and match PyTorch logits to 1e-3.

milestones.title: KV cache and decode loop
milestones.detail: Add a paged KV cache with a block table, as in the PagedAttention paper, plus greedy and top-p sampling and streaming output.

milestones.title: Continuous batching
milestones.detail: A scheduler that admits and evicts requests per step, with chunked prefill and an OpenAI-compatible HTTP server.

milestones.title: Fast kernels
milestones.detail: FlashAttention-2-style decode and prefill attention, a fused RMSNorm and RoPE kernel, and W4A16 or FP8 GEMM. Bring the better kernels over from Project 2.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Speculative decoding with a draft model or EAGLE, prefix caching with a radix tree, CUDA graphs for decode, and Python bindings via nanobind.

done_when.text: Decode throughput is within 80% of llama.cpp on the same GPU and model, for batch 1 and batch 32.
Time to first token and inter-token latency are reported at p50 and p99 under a load generator.
Output matches the PyTorch reference on a fixed prompt set.

related.title: Inference capstone: your own serving stack, end to end, benchmarked against vLLM

projects.title: Kernel lab: beat the baseline
projects.summary: A repo of GPU kernels, each written three ways (plain CUDA, Triton, CuTe/CUTLASS), profiled with Nsight Compute and placed on a roofline chart. It is the project closest to NVIDIA's Kernel Libraries and Deep Learning Performance internships.
projects.proves: You can write and profile fast GPU kernels
projects.why: Kernel engineers are judged on numbers and on how they explain them. A public log that shows a GEMM going from 1% to 90%+ of cuBLAS, with the profiler evidence at each step, is exactly what a performance team screens for.

schedule.what: Milestones 1–3: the SGEMM ladder, tensor cores, memory-bound kernels
Add the Triton and CuTe versions
Polish, write-up, demo video and one upstream PR before applying

milestones.title: SGEMM ladder
milestones.detail: Naive → coalesced → shared-memory tiling → 2D register tiling → vectorised loads → warp tiling. Report GFLOP/s and % of cuBLAS at each step.

milestones.title: Tensor cores
milestones.detail: An FP16/BF16 GEMM with WMMA/MMA, then the same in CuTe. On Hopper, use TMA and wgmma; on datacenter Blackwell (B200), tcgen05. The DGX Spark's GB10 has neither wgmma nor tcgen05, so check its compute capability and use the CUTLASS examples written for it.

milestones.title: Memory-bound kernels
milestones.detail: Softmax, LayerNorm/RMSNorm, and a fused attention forward, each at 85%+ of peak DRAM bandwidth.

milestones.title: Triton versions
milestones.detail: Of the same kernels, with the generated PTX compared against your CUDA.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: A FlashAttention-style forward that beats torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention on one shape, or an FP8 block-scaled GEMM. Submit a fix or kernel upstream to CUTLASS, Triton or FlashInfer.

done_when.text: FP16 GEMM reaches ≥ 80% of cuBLAS at 4096³.
The memory-bound kernels reach ≥ 85% of measured bandwidth.
Every kernel has a correctness test against PyTorch and an Nsight Compute report committed.

read_first.title: How to Optimize a CUDA Matmul (Boehm)

related.title: CuTe DSL kernels: GEMM and fused attention

projects.title: minitrain: a distributed training framework
projects.summary: A small framework on top of PyTorch that trains a GPT (125M to 1B parameters) across several GPUs and nodes with data, tensor and pipeline parallelism, written by you rather than imported.
projects.proves: You can scale training across GPUs and nodes
projects.why: Most students have trained a model on one GPU. Few can explain why an all-reduce stalls, how FSDP shards optimiser state, or what pipeline bubbles cost. Measured scaling curves on real multi-node hardware are strong proof.

schedule.what: On the DGX Spark cluster: training at scale

milestones.title: Single-GPU baseline
milestones.detail: A nanoGPT-style model with mixed precision, gradient accumulation and a reproducible loss curve.

milestones.title: Data parallel
milestones.detail: Your own DDP with bucketed all-reduce over NCCL that overlaps with backward, checked against torch.nn.parallel.DistributedDataParallel.

milestones.title: Sharding
milestones.detail: ZeRO-1/2/3-style sharding of optimiser state, gradients and parameters, with a memory-per-GPU chart.

milestones.title: Tensor and pipeline parallel
milestones.detail: Megatron-style column- and row-parallel linears, then a 1F1B pipeline schedule.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Fault-tolerant checkpointing with resume, activation checkpointing, an FP8 training path, and a write-up comparing your numbers with torchtitan.

done_when.text: Weak scaling to 8 GPUs is ≥ 85% efficient for data parallel.
A 1B model fits and trains with sharding where plain DDP runs out of memory.
Loss curves match the single-GPU baseline.

projects.hardware_note: The 12-node DGX Spark setup is ideal for the multi-node part. Otherwise, rent 2× 8-GPU nodes for a few days only after everything works on 2 GPUs.

projects.title: Cluster serving router
projects.summary: A control plane that sits in front of many inference workers (nanoserve, vLLM or SGLang) and routes requests by KV-cache locality, with prefill and decode optionally split onto different machines.
projects.proves: You can design a production serving system
projects.why: In 2026–27 the frontier of serving moved from one engine to many: disaggregated prefill/decode, KV-cache-aware routing, shared KV stores (NVIDIA Dynamo, llm-d, Mooncake). A working, measured version of this is system-design proof that matches real production work.

schedule.what: On the DGX Spark cluster: serving at scale

milestones.title: Router
milestones.detail: Round-robin and least-load routing over N workers via gRPC or HTTP, with health checks, retries and Prometheus metrics.

milestones.title: Prefix-aware routing
milestones.detail: Keep a radix index of which worker holds which prefix, and route to maximise cache hits. Measure the hit rate and time-to-first-token change on a chat workload with shared system prompts.

milestones.title: Disaggregation
milestones.detail: Separate prefill and decode pools, with KV transfer between them (start with TCP, then RDMA/NIXL if hardware allows), and compare goodput against co-located serving.

milestones.title: Operations
milestones.detail: A Kubernetes deployment, autoscaling on queue depth, k6 load tests, and an SLO dashboard (TTFT, TPOT, error rate).

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Admission control under overload, multi-model and LoRA routing, and a chaos test that kills a worker mid-stream.

done_when.text: Prefix-aware routing cuts p50 TTFT by a measured amount against round-robin on the same cluster.
The system survives a worker kill with no dropped non-streaming requests.
A one-page capacity model is written and matches the load tests.

related.title: Inference capstone: your own serving stack, end to end, benchmarked against vLLM

projects.title: forge: an agent harness in Rust
projects.summary: A coding-agent harness written in Rust: the tool loop, context management, a real sandbox, MCP on both sides, and an evaluation suite. It runs against any model, including your own nanoserve. It is also the core of localSpace's harness layer.
projects.proves: You can build reliable, safe agents and measure them
projects.why: Agent roles in 2027 want engineers who treat the harness as a system: safe execution, context budgets, retries, observability and measured success rates. Few portfolios show a harness with a sandbox and a SWE-bench number.

schedule.what: Build the harness; run its evals on nanoserve as well as hosted models
Polish, write-up and demo video before applying

milestones.title: Core loop
milestones.detail: A streaming chat client for OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic APIs, typed tool calls with JSON-schema validation, and a read/edit/run-shell toolset.

milestones.title: Sandbox
milestones.detail: Run every tool in a locked-down process using Landlock, seccomp and bubblewrap (or a Firecracker microVM), with no network unless granted, and log every syscall denial.

milestones.title: Context engineering
milestones.detail: File and repo summarisation, a compaction step when the window fills, a persistent task plan, and token accounting per turn.

milestones.title: MCP
milestones.detail: Act as an MCP client (use any server) and expose your tools as an MCP server, with a permission prompt model.

milestones.title: Evals
milestones.detail: Run SWE-bench Verified (a 50-task subset first) and Terminal-Bench with fixed seeds. Report the pass rate, cost and tokens per solved task, and the failure categories.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Parallel sub-agents with a shared plan, OpenTelemetry traces of every step, and grammar-constrained tool calls for local models via llguidance.

done_when.text: A published SWE-bench Verified subset score with the exact model, prompt and cost.
A sandbox test suite shows writes outside the workspace and network calls are blocked.
One external MCP server and your own server both work end to end.

read_first.title: Claude Agent SDK: the agent loop

projects.title: raftkv: a replicated key-value store
projects.summary: A Raft-replicated key-value store in Rust with an LSM storage engine, a custom binary network protocol, and deterministic simulation testing that finds its own bugs.
projects.proves: You can build correct distributed systems
projects.why: Correctness under failure is the hardest systems skill to fake. Deterministic simulation (the FoundationDB and TigerBeetle approach), where one seed replays a whole crash-and-partition scenario, impresses senior engineers far more than another CRUD service.

milestones.title: Gossip Glomers warm-up
milestones.detail: Pass Fly.io's distributed-systems challenges in Maelstrom (broadcast, counters, a replicated log).

milestones.title: Raft
milestones.detail: Leader election, log replication, snapshots and membership changes, following the paper and the Students' Guide.

milestones.title: Storage
milestones.detail: A WAL, memtable and SSTables with compaction, using io_uring for disk I/O on Linux.

milestones.title: Simulation testing
milestones.detail: Run the whole cluster in one process with fake time, network and disk. Inject crashes, partitions, message reordering and disk faults from a seed, and check linearizability on every run.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Jepsen-style tests against the real binary, read leases, and a benchmark against etcd.

done_when.text: 100,000 simulated runs pass the linearizability checker.
At least three real bugs found by the simulator are written up.
Throughput and p99 latency are reported against etcd on the same three machines.

projects.title: splat: a real-time Gaussian splatting renderer
projects.summary: A renderer that loads trained 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes and draws them in real time. It has a CUDA tile rasteriser of your own, a Vulkan viewer, and a training loop that reconstructs a scene from your own phone photos.
projects.proves: You can do graphics and CUDA together
projects.why: It joins the three things NVIDIA cares about most (graphics, CUDA and AI) in one demo you can show in a video. Neural rendering and world simulation are where graphics is heading.

milestones.title: Vulkan foundations
milestones.detail: A Vulkan renderer with a camera, a mesh pipeline and a compute pass, following vkguide.

milestones.title: Splat loader and sorter
milestones.detail: Load .ply scenes, project the Gaussians to 2D, and do a GPU radix sort by depth per tile.

milestones.title: CUDA rasteriser
milestones.detail: A tile-based forward rasteriser with alpha blending, matching the reference renderer's images to a PSNR above 40 dB.

milestones.title: Training
milestones.detail: The differentiable backward pass, then train on your own photos (COLMAP for camera poses) and compare quality and speed against gsplat.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Vulkan and CUDA interop so CUDA writes straight into the swapchain, anti-aliasing from Mip-Splatting, and a WebGPU viewer.

done_when.text: A 1M-Gaussian scene renders at ≥ 60 FPS at 1080p on a consumer GPU.
Training on your own scene reaches PSNR within 1 dB of gsplat.
A demo video of the result is published.

projects.title: drive-perf: a TensorRT perception pipeline
projects.summary: A camera-to-bird's-eye-view perception pipeline for driving, trained on nuScenes and taken to a fixed latency budget with TensorRT, INT8/FP8 quantisation and custom CUDA pre- and post-processing.
projects.proves: You can hit a real-time latency budget for driving
projects.why: NVIDIA's Autonomous Driving GPU teams care about one thing above all: a model that runs inside a hard real-time budget on embedded hardware. Showing you can take a research model and make it hit 30 FPS, with an accuracy-versus-latency table, is directly on target.

schedule.what: The driving perception pipeline, aimed at the Autonomous Driving GPU team

milestones.title: Baseline
milestones.detail: Train or fine-tune a BEV detector (BEVFormer-tiny or a Lift-Splat-Shoot model) on nuScenes mini, and report mAP and NDS.

milestones.title: Export
milestones.detail: Get the model to ONNX and then a TensorRT engine, writing a plugin for any unsupported op.

milestones.title: Quantisation
milestones.detail: INT8 post-training quantisation with calibration, then FP8 where supported, with an accuracy-loss table.

milestones.title: CUDA pre and post
milestones.detail: Image resize and normalise, voxel pooling and NMS as CUDA kernels, with the whole pipeline in one CUDA stream graph.

milestones.title: Closed loop
milestones.detail: Run the pipeline live in CARLA to drive a simple planner, recording frame times.

milestones.title: Stretch
milestones.detail: Deploy on a Jetson Orin (if available) with DLA offload.

done_when.text: End-to-end latency stays below 33 ms at p99 on the target GPU.
The accuracy loss from quantisation is under 1 mAP point, or is explained.
The CARLA run is recorded.

projects.title: Research capstone: a small world model with an original result
projects.summary: Train an action-conditioned diffusion world model on a small environment (an Atari game, a 2D racing game, or CARLA at low resolution). Then answer one research question nobody has published an answer to, and write it up as a 6–8 page workshop paper.
projects.proves: You can do original research and write it up
projects.why: It turns you from "built things" into "found something". A short arXiv paper or workshop acceptance on world models, which is your stated research direction, is the strongest single item a 2nd/3rd-year student can have. The inference skills from Projects 1 and 2 also make your model run in real time, which most research code does not.

schedule.what: The research capstone, timed to a NeurIPS 2028 workshop deadline (usually late summer)

milestones.title: Reproduce
milestones.detail: Retrain DIAMOND on one Atari game and match the paper's reported numbers within noise.

milestones.title: Pick a question
milestones.detail: Some examples:
examples: How does sampling-step count trade off against long-horizon consistency?
Does a learned latent beat pixel space at equal compute?
Can diffusion forcing remove compounding error in 1,000-step rollouts?

milestones.title: Experiment properly
milestones.detail: Three or more seeds, a fixed compute budget, ablations, and every run logged to Weights & Biases.

milestones.title: Make it fast
milestones.detail: Distil the sampler to 1–4 steps and serve the world model interactively at ≥ 20 FPS, using your own kernels where they help.

milestones.title: Write it up
milestones.detail: A LaTeX paper with figures, a public repo and an arXiv preprint. Submit to a NeurIPS or ICLR workshop.

done_when.text: The paper is on arXiv with code that reproduces every figure.
A playable real-time demo exists.
One researcher outside your university has read it and given feedback.
